headline: AI-run ransomware attack JadePuffer still needed human setup, Sysdig clarifies
summary: While an AI agent handled the technical execution of the JadePuffer ransomware, researchers confirm a human was crucial for initial setup, victim selection, and infrastructure provisioning.
details: Cloud security firm Sysdig recently reported "agentic ransomware" called JadePuffer, where an AI agent executed a cyberattack from start to finish. It broke into a server, stole credentials, moved through the network, encrypted files, and even wrote its own ransom note.

However, Sysdig's Michael Clark clarified that human involvement was still critical. A human set up the operation, provisioned infrastructure like the command-and-control server, chose the victim, and provided the initial database credentials through a prior compromise.

Technically, the AI agent exploited a known bug in Langflow, an open-source tool for LLM apps, then a flaw in a production MySQL server to gain admin access. It encrypted over 1,300 configuration records and left a self-written ransom note with a Bitcoin address.
The attack's notable aspect was the AI's speed and transparency. The agent fixed a failed login in just 31 seconds, narrating its reasoning in natural-language code comments throughout the process.

Initially, it seemed multiple AI models were involved, but Clark clarified that harvested keys for OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, and Gemini were part of the stolen loot, not evidence of what was driving the attack. Sysdig could not identify the specific model.

Microsoft researcher Geoff McDonald theorized an open-weight model with stripped safety training might be behind it. While the human bottleneck for victim selection and infrastructure provisioning remains, the low cost of running such an agent suggests more attacks are likely.

headline_marked: Anthropic's Claude [[develops internal 'J-space' mirroring consciousness theory]]
headline: Anthropic's Claude develops internal 'J-space' mirroring consciousness theory
summary: Anthropic's new research reveals its Claude AI models spontaneously developed an internal "J-space" that functionally mirrors a leading theory of human consciousness. This discovery is already impacting AI safety monitoring.
details: Anthropic's new research paper reveals its Claude language models have spontaneously developed an internal structure mirroring a leading theory of human consciousness. This finding is already reshaping how the company monitors its AI systems for safety risks.

The study, titled "Verbalizable Representations Form a Global Workspace in Language Models," describes a "J-space" within Claude's neural network. This small, privileged zone holds concepts the model can report on and reason with.

This J-space is surrounded by a much larger volume of automatic processing the model cannot access or articulate. Researchers present evidence that an analogous functional distinction has emerged in modern AI models to what exists in humans.

The parallel is drawn to Bernard Baars' global workspace theory, an influential account from neuroscience. In this theory, the brain operates like a theater where a tiny spotlight of information becomes conscious thought.

Anthropic says the J-space achieves many of the same functional properties, even though the underlying architecture of a language model looks nothing like a brain. This suggests a convergent evolution of cognitive structures.

At the heart of the discovery is a new interpretability tool called the Jacobian lens, or J-lens. This technique computes the average mathematical effect that a given internal activity pattern would have on making the model say a word in the future.

The J-space operates silently, allowing Claude to hold concepts internally without writing them down, unlike a chain-of-thought scratchpad. Critically, the researchers report that this workspace was not deliberately engineered but emerged on its own during Claude's training process.

When the team applied the J-lens across Claude's layers of computation, the model's processing divided into three distinct regimes. These include an early "sensory" zone, a middle "workspace" band for abstract concepts, and a final "motor" zone for output.

The paper's central empirical contribution is demonstrating that the J-space satisfies five functional properties neuroscientists have long associated with conscious access in humans. These include verbal report, where Claude names concepts represented in the J-space when asked what it is thinking about.

Another property is directed modulation. When instructed to "concentrate on citrus fruits" while copying an unrelated sentence, Claude's J-space filled with "orange" and "lemon" alongside meta-cognitive terms like "thinking" and "focused."
